labels.rationale: The whole piece fits a natural-minor set on E at 0.98, and the tool key Em, the commonest chord root and the longest section (chorus, E/Nahawand) all support E. The two melody cues and the melody-only analysis point at F# instead, and the pre-chorus shows an E/B split, so the relative F# reading is recorded rather than dropped. 12-TET cannot separate this set from Bayati with its 2nd rounded up, so the name is only consistent, at low confidence.

Phrase endings (75% of final notes, 62% of last notes) and the commonest chord root place the tonic on C, and the C-Db-Eb-F-G-Bb set fits Kurd at 0.97 in both the full and the melody-only analysis. The tool declares Fm and the other voice says F, so the tonic may really be F a fifth up, where the same notes read as Nahawand; the 6th degree is almost never sung, which leaves the shape under-determined. Bayati with the 2nd rounded down gives the same 12-TET notes, so the name is consistent only.

Whole piece, verse, chorus and the melody-only cross-check all read D on a natural-minor set with a fit of 0.98-1.00, so the shape is stable across sections; the tool key Dm and phrase endings on D agree. The strongest competing reading is the relative A as Kurd/Phrygian (fit 1.00), which the other voice also suggests, and C and Bb fit equally well as relative readings. The analyzer rates the tonic low and 12-TET cannot separate Nahawand from Bayati, so the name stays consistent at low confidence.

Three of the four cues (most-used note, tool key and chord root, other voice) plus the chorus put the tonic on E, and the natural-minor set fits at 1.00 in both the full and the melody-only analysis. Phrase endings land on B in 64% of cases and the verse is read as B/Kurd with a tonic/dominant split, so B is kept as the alternative tonic instead of being decided away. Bayati rounds to these same notes in ABC, so Nahawand is consistent, not established.

Phrase endings, the tool key Bm and the other voice agree on B, and the B-C-D-E-F#-G set fits Kurd at 1.00 in both the full and the melody-only analysis, which is why the tonic keeps the analyzer's high rating. The E pitch class is the most used of all and the chorus is read as E/Nahawand with an E/B split, so a fourth-up reading of the chorus is recorded as the alternative tonic. Shape confidence is capped at medium by 12-TET input and Bayati gives the same notes, so overall confidence is medium.

The whole piece fits a natural-minor set at 1.00 and the declared key is Em, but the tonic margin is 0.01: the most-used note and the phrase endings point elsewhere and the melody-only analysis reads A as a non-maqam Dorian shape. The verse is read as A and the chorus as B/Kurd, so the sections disagree about the tonic and a different tonic would change the name. The 6th degree is thin, which leaves Nahawand, Dorian and B-Kurd indistinguishable, so the name is only possible at low confidence.

The D-Eb-F-G-A-Bb set fits Kurd at 1.00 in the whole piece, the chorus, the bridge and the melody-only analysis, and the tool key Dm plus the other voice support the tonic D. The most-used note and the phrase endings both fall on F, and the verse is read as F with no standard maqam name, so a relative F reading is recorded as an alternative tonic. Nahawand and Bayati share these notes after 12-TET rounding, so the Kurd name is consistent only and the analyzer's low tonic rating is kept.

This mix version yields almost the same evidence as the album cut: phrase endings and the commonest chord root place the tonic on C, and the set fits Kurd at 0.97 in both the full and the melody-only analysis. The tool declares Fm and the other voice says F, so the fifth relationships are kept as alternatives and the 6th degree is again almost absent, leaving the shape under-determined. Bayati with its 2nd rounded down produces the same notes, so the name is consistent only at low confidence.
